title: Festivals and everyday culture
job: Talk about what is happening around you
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 4.5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedTenses: present — what happens every year, and what happens this week
present with the impersonal si, L3-M8's, describing what is done

rules.text: CHE IS THE RELATIVE PRONOUN, AND IT IS ONE WORD FOR ALL OF ENGLISH'S. who, which and that are all che; it does not care whether it stands for a person or a thing, nor whether that person is doing the verb or having it done to them. È una festa che mi piace · le persone che lavorano qui · il regalo che ho comprato. L1-M5 opened che for the reported clause and L3-M3 gave it the opinion job; this is the same word doing a third job, and it is the first job in the ladder that cannot be done without it.

AFTER A PREPOSITION, CHE BECOMES CUI. la festa di cui parlo ("the festival I am talking about"), la persona con cui lavoro, il paese in cui vivo. English can bury the preposition at the end of the clause — "the festival I am talking about" — and Italian never can: the preposition goes in front, and che cannot follow it. That is the whole of the addition.

THE ARTICLE IS THE TENSE. domenica on its own means THIS Sunday; la domenica means EVERY Sunday. Domenica vado a Roma against La domenica non lavoro. Spanish marks the same difference the same way, and English needs whole extra words — "on Sunday" against "on Sundays". The second half of the trap is that a bare day takes NO preposition at all in Italian: never a domenica, never in domenica.

A DATE IS IL PLUS THE PLAIN NUMBER PLUS THE MONTH: il quindici agosto, il venticinque dicembre. Only the first of the month takes an ordinal — il primo gennaio — and every other day is the cardinal you already know. Months and days of the week are written in LOWERCASE in Italian, which an English habit will capitalise every time.

L3-M8'S IMPERSONAL SI IS HOW A CUSTOM IS DESCRIBED, because a custom has no doer: a Natale si mangia il panettone, a Ferragosto si chiude tutto. Nothing new is opened here — it is M8's shape pointed at the calendar, which is what leaves room in this module for the months and the festivals themselves.

sentences.display: È una festa che mi piace molto
sentences.cue: It is a festival that I like a lot
sentences.literal: It-is a festival that to-me it-pleases much

words.note: Feminine, and it covers both a public festival and a private party. fare festa is to celebrate; giorno di festa is a public holiday.

sentences.trap: English can drop the relative word altogether — "a festival I like a lot" — and Italian cannot. The che is compulsory, however short the clause is.
sentences.sound: e OO-na FES-ta ke mee PYA-che MOL-to. che is one syllable, k plus e, never ch as in church.

variations.display: Non è una festa che mi piace
variations.cue: It is not a festival that I like
variations.changed: negative

variations.display: È una festa che mi piace poco
variations.cue: It is a festival I do not much like
variations.changed: how much, using L1-M4's poco

variations.display: Sono feste che mi piacciono
variations.cue: They are festivals that I like
variations.changed: plural, so both verbs move

mistake.display: È una festa mi piace molto
mistake.why: Italian never drops the relative word: È una festa che mi piace molto.

sentences.usage: How you answer when somebody asks what a festival in your own country is like.
sentences.mnemonic: che is never optional in Italian.

sentences.display: Le persone che lavorano qui sono gentili
sentences.cue: The people who work here are kind
sentences.literal: The people that they-work here they-are kind

words.note: Feminine and countable: due persone. L2-M10's gente means people as a mass and takes a singular verb, which persone never does.
The they-form of L1-M4's lavoro and lavora. The relative clause needs a plural verb here because le persone is plural.

sentences.trap: English picks who for people and which for things. Italian does not choose: che covers both, and reaching for chi here would turn the sentence into a question.
sentences.sound: le per-SO-ne ke la-VO-ra-no kwee SO-no jen-TEE-lee. lavorano is stressed on the VO, three syllables before the end.

variations.display: Le persone che lavorano qui sono poche
variations.cue: The people who work here are few
variations.changed: what is said about them

variations.display: La persona che lavora qui è gentile
variations.cue: The person who works here is kind
variations.changed: singular, so all three words move

variations.display: Le persone che vedo qui sono gentili
variations.cue: The people I see here are kind
variations.changed: che as the object of the clause instead of its subject

mistake.display: Le persone chi lavorano qui sono gentili
mistake.why: chi asks a question; the relative word is che: Le persone che lavorano qui sono gentili.

sentences.usage: An ordinary compliment about a workplace, a shop or a neighbourhood.

sentences.display: La festa di cui parlo è il quindici agosto
sentences.cue: The festival I am talking about is on the fifteenth of August
sentences.literal: The festival of which I-speak is the fifteen August

words.note: What che becomes after a preposition: di cui, con cui, in cui. It never stands alone and never starts a sentence.
Lowercase, like every Italian month. The fifteenth of August is Ferragosto and most of the country stops for it.

sentences.trap: English puts the preposition at the end — "the festival I'm talking about" — and an Italian sentence built that way has nowhere to put the di. It goes in front of cui, always.
sentences.sound: la FES-ta dee KOO-ee PAR-lo e eel KWEEN-dee-chee a-GOS-to. cui is two vowels run together, koo-ee.

variations.display: La persona con cui lavoro è gentile
variations.cue: The person I work with is kind
variations.changed: a different preposition in front of cui

variations.display: La festa di cui parlo è il primo gennaio
variations.cue: The festival I am talking about is on the first of January
variations.changed: the one date that takes an ordinal

variations.display: La festa che mi piace è il quindici agosto
variations.cue: The festival I like is on the fifteenth of August
variations.changed: no preposition, so che comes back

mistake.display: La festa di che parlo è il quindici agosto
mistake.why: che cannot follow a preposition: La festa di cui parlo è il quindici agosto.

sentences.usage: Said while explaining a festival to somebody who has never heard of it.
sentences.mnemonic: Preposition in front, and che turns into cui.

sentences.cue: The first of January is New Year's Day

words.note: Lowercase. a gennaio and in gennaio both mean "in January" and both are said.
Literally "head of the year", written as one word and capitalised because it names a specific day.

sentences.trap: This is the single date in the month that takes an ordinal. il primo gennaio, but il due gennaio and il tre gennaio — never il secondo gennaio.
sentences.sound: eel PREE-mo jen-NA-yo e ka-po-DAN-no. gennaio starts with a soft j and holds its double n.

variations.display: Il quindici agosto è Ferragosto
variations.cue: The fifteenth of August is Ferragosto
variations.changed: a plain number, because it is not the first

variations.display: A gennaio non c'è una festa
variations.cue: In January there is no festival
variations.changed: the month on its own, with no date

variations.display: Il primo gennaio non si lavora
variations.cue: Nobody works on the first of January
variations.changed: what is done, with M8's impersonal si

mistake.why: Months are lowercase in Italian: Il primo gennaio è Capodanno.

sentences.usage: Explaining the calendar to somebody new, or checking a date out loud.
sentences.mnemonic: Only the first is an ordinal.

sentences.display: A Natale si mangia il panettone

words.note: Capitalised, and it takes a: a Natale, the same little a as a Pasqua and a Ferragosto. Buon Natale is the greeting.
The tall sweet bread of Christmas, masculine. Milan claims it; the argument with pandoro is annual and unresolved.

sentences.trap: English needs a subject — "people eat", "we eat", "you eat" — and a learner picks one, usually the wrong one. A custom has no doer, so Italian uses M8's si and names nobody.
sentences.sound: a na-TA-le see MAN-ja eel pa-net-TO-ne. panettone holds its double t.

variations.display: A Pasqua si mangia bene
variations.cue: At Easter people eat well
variations.changed: a different festival

variations.display: A Natale non si lavora
variations.cue: Nobody works at Christmas
variations.changed: negative, and what is not done

variations.display: A casa mia si mangia il panettone
variations.cue: At my house we eat panettone
variations.changed: a place instead of a festival

mistake.display: A Natale mangiamo il panettone tutti
mistake.why: A custom takes the impersonal: A Natale si mangia il panettone.

sentences.usage: How anybody describes their own country's customs to a visitor.
sentences.mnemonic: A custom has no doer, so it takes si.

words.note: The fifteenth of August, and the day the country stops. Shops, offices and whole towns close, which is why it is worth a sentence of its own.
M8's impersonal si on chiudere. One thing, si chiude; several things, si chiudono, exactly as with si vende and si vendono.
Everything, as one mass. It stays singular here, which is why the verb beside it does too.

sentences.trap: tutto counts as one thing, so the verb is singular — si chiude, not si chiudono. English "everything closes" happens to agree, but "all the shops close" does not, and that is where the plural is needed.
sentences.sound: a fer-ra-GOS-to see KYOO-de TOOT-to. chiude begins with a hard k sound.

variations.display: A Ferragosto si chiudono le farmacie
variations.cue: At Ferragosto the pharmacies close
variations.changed: a plural thing, so the verb goes plural

variations.display: A Natale si chiude tutto
variations.cue: At Christmas everything closes
variations.changed: a different festival

variations.display: La domenica si chiude tutto
variations.cue: On Sundays everything closes
variations.changed: every Sunday instead of a festival

mistake.why: tutto is singular: A Ferragosto si chiude tutto.

sentences.usage: The single most useful warning you can give a visitor arriving in mid-August.
sentences.mnemonic: tutto is one thing, however much it contains.

sentences.display: La domenica non lavoro, ma domenica vado a Roma
sentences.cue: On Sundays I do not work, but this Sunday I am going to Rome
sentences.literal: The Sunday not I-work, but Sunday I-go to Rome

words.note: The article makes it habitual. Bare domenica, L2-M6's word, means this coming Sunday. L1-M4's il lunedì and il sabato work the same way.

sentences.trap: English marks the difference with a plural and a preposition — "on Sundays" against "on Sunday" — and Italian marks it with one three-letter article. There is no preposition in either half.
sentences.sound: la do-ME-nee-ka non la-VO-ro, ma do-ME-nee-ka VA-do a RO-ma. The two domenica sound identical; only the la separates them.

variations.display: La domenica non si lavora
variations.cue: Nobody works on Sundays
variations.changed: the impersonal, so nobody is named

variations.display: Domenica vado a Roma
variations.cue: This Sunday I am going to Rome
variations.changed: only the one-off half

variations.display: La domenica mangiamo a casa
variations.cue: On Sundays we eat at home
variations.changed: a habit with a plural subject

mistake.why: A day of the week takes no preposition in Italian: La domenica non lavoro.

sentences.usage: The sentence that sorts out a diary — habit first, then the exception.

sentences.display: Il mio compleanno è il quindici dicembre
sentences.cue: My birthday is on the fifteenth of December
sentences.literal: The my birthday is the fifteen December

words.note: Masculine, and it keeps its article after the possessive: il mio compleanno. Buon compleanno is the greeting.
Lowercase. The months ending in -bre are settembre, ottobre, novembre and dicembre, all stressed on the syllable before the ending.

sentences.trap: Italian keeps the article in front of the possessive — il mio compleanno — where English drops it. This is L2-M2's law, and a birthday is where a learner most often forgets it.
sentences.sound: eel MEE-o kom-ple-AN-no e eel KWEEN-dee-chee dee-CHEM-bre. compleanno holds its double n.

variations.display: Il mio compleanno è a dicembre
variations.cue: My birthday is in December
variations.changed: the month only, with no date

variations.display: Il suo compleanno è il primo gennaio
variations.cue: His birthday is on the first of January
variations.changed: somebody else, and the ordinal date

variations.display: A Natale è anche il mio compleanno
variations.cue: My birthday is at Christmas too
variations.changed: the date given as a festival instead

mistake.display: Mio compleanno è il quindici dicembre
mistake.why: The article stays in front of the possessive: Il mio compleanno è il quindici dicembre.

sentences.usage: Asked and answered constantly, and the easiest date in the language to practise.

sentences.display: In agosto c'è una sagra nel mio paese
sentences.cue: In August there is a food festival in my village
sentences.literal: In August there-is a food-festival in-the my village

words.note: A village festival built around one food — la sagra del pesce, la sagra della porchetta. It is not a festa and there is no English word for it.
Two meanings in one word: the small town you are from, and the country as a whole. Context decides, and a sagra always means the first.

sentences.trap: sagra and festa are not interchangeable. A sagra is small, local and about eating one particular thing, and calling Ferragosto a sagra would puzzle anybody.
sentences.sound: een a-GOS-to che OO-na SA-gra nel MEE-o pa-E-ze. paese is three syllables, stressed on the E.

variations.display: A Natale c'è una festa nel mio paese
variations.cue: At Christmas there is a festival in my village
variations.changed: a festival instead of a sagra

variations.display: In agosto ci sono due sagre
variations.cue: In August there are two food festivals
variations.changed: plural, so c'è becomes ci sono

variations.display: La sagra di cui parlo è in agosto
variations.cue: The food festival I am talking about is in August
variations.changed: introduced with cui

mistake.display: In agosto c'è una festa nel mio paese di cibo
mistake.why: Italian has a single word for it: In agosto c'è una sagra nel mio paese.

sentences.usage: How anybody from a small Italian town describes their summer.
sentences.mnemonic: A sagra is a festival with a menu.

sentences.display: Chi lavora a Pasqua non fa festa
sentences.cue: Whoever works at Easter does not celebrate
sentences.literal: Who works at Easter not makes festival

words.note: Two jobs: the question word (chi è?) and "whoever", standing on its own with no noun in front. It is never the relative che.
Capitalised, and it takes a: a Pasqua. The Monday after it is Pasquetta, and most of the country spends it outdoors.

sentences.trap: chi and che are the pair this module keeps apart. chi carries its own noun inside it — "the person who" — while che needs one in front: le persone che lavorano.
sentences.sound: kee la-VO-ra a PAS-kwa non fa FES-ta. chi is kee, with a hard k.

variations.display: Chi lavora a Natale non fa festa
variations.cue: Whoever works at Christmas does not celebrate
variations.changed: a different festival

variations.display: Chi è quella persona?
variations.cue: Who is that person?
variations.changed: chi doing its question job

variations.display: Le persone che lavorano a Pasqua sono poche
variations.cue: Few people work at Easter
variations.changed: che with a noun in front of it, instead of chi

mistake.display: Che lavora a Pasqua non fa festa
mistake.why: che needs a noun in front of it; standing alone the word is chi: Chi lavora a Pasqua non fa festa.

sentences.usage: A dry observation about working over a holiday — said with sympathy, usually.
sentences.mnemonic: chi already contains its noun; che needs one.
